brief-1.text: Question-bank harvesting. Each paper shows 60 of only 90 questions (two-thirds of the bank; any two papers share about 40 questions), the exam stays open from Friday 08:00 to Monday 08:00, and resitters draw from the same bank, so early or repeat candidates can reconstruct and circulate most of the bank. The shuffling and 'no two papers are the same' give little protection. A strong reply flags this and proposes a much larger bank, a short fixed sitting window, or both.

Proxy test-taking goes undetected. The ID snapshot is only looked at if the session is flagged, the flags target behaviour rather than identity, and nothing in the design compares the snapshot with a reference photo or the booking. A calm expert sitting the exam in someone else's name is never checked. A strong reply says identity must be verified on every session against an independent reference, not only on flagged ones.

The disconnect rule is an exploit. When the connection drops the timer pauses and nothing streams, reconnections are unlimited, and the candidate has already seen the question, so pulling the cable buys unlimited unmonitored, untimed time to look up answers or consult someone. A strong reply caps paused time and reconnections, hides the current question or records locally on disconnect, and reviews sessions with drops.

Certification comes before review. Passes are confirmed and put on the public register two working days after the exam, but flagged sessions are reviewed within ten working days, so a flagged cheat is certified and can sign fire-door reports before anyone looks, with no stated revocation process. A strong reply holds results for flagged sessions until review and defines revocation.

brief-2.text: The setup PIN is public. Controllers broadcast 'K3-' plus the serial over Bluetooth and the PIN is the serial's last six digits, so anyone within Bluetooth range (for example from a public road) can enter setup mode and turn frost protection off, change thresholds or run valves; the dashboard only texts when frost protection starts or a unit goes offline, so nobody is alerted. The label inside the lid gives no protection. A strong reply calls for a random per-device secret or physical presence check, stopping the serial broadcast, and alerts on setting changes.

Ownership-claim takeover. A claim needs only serial numbers, which anyone can collect from Bluetooth adverts or labels, and it succeeds by default after seven days unless the previous owner answers an email (which may go to an old or unmonitored address). An attacker can gain remote control of another farm's controllers. A strong reply requires proof of physical possession (a code from the device or a button press) and positive confirmation rather than silence as consent.

Shared fleet secret. Every unit uses the same API key, built into firmware that is published on the website, and serials are easy to collect, so anyone who extracts the key can impersonate any controller to the cloud (feed false readings, keep a unit looking online, receive its commands). A strong reply calls for unique per-device credentials, ideally in secure hardware, with revocation.

Update timing and blast radius. All controllers install and reboot at 02:00, inside the pre-dawn hours when frost protection is most needed, and every unit takes a new release the same night, so one faulty or malicious signed release, or a failed reboot, can leave sprinklers off across the fleet on a frost night. A strong reply defers updates when frost risk is present or sprinklers are running, stages rollouts, and keeps a fallback image.

brief-3.text: The bank-change checks are self-referential. Suppliers can edit their email, phone and bank details in the same profile, and both the confirmation email and the AP callback use those profile values, so anyone who takes over a supplier login (for example via the email password reset after compromising the supplier's mailbox) changes the phone and email first and then confirms the bank change to themselves. A strong reply requires a callback to an independently held number, notice to the previous contacts, and a hold on changes made together.

One person can pay a supplier end to end. A site manager can add a subcontractor, raise purchase orders up to £25,000 alone, and invoices under £10,000 that match an open order are paid with no further human approval (larger amounts can be split under the threshold). A site manager with a sham or connected company gets paid with no second person involved; the registry check only proves the company exists, not that it is independent or that the bank account is its own. A strong reply separates supplier set-up from ordering, requires someone else to confirm work received, and checks links between staff and suppliers.

Payment-file tampering. The CSV sits on the finance shared drive between export and upload, and the financial controller's approval shows only the count and total, so changing account numbers or payees in the file (by the supervisor or anyone with write access to the drive) leaves both unchanged and passes approval. A strong reply calls for direct integration or a locked, integrity-checked file, restricted access, and approval or reconciliation at payee and account level against the supplier master.

Weak duplicate detection. Blocking only an exact repeat of an invoice number from the same supplier lets the same invoice be paid twice with a changed number or format, or through a second supplier record, and auto-approval under £10,000 means no human sees it. A strong reply adds duplicate checks on amount, date, purchase order and bank account, and checks for duplicate supplier records.
